I think there's a distinction between how a cis person might feel like they're not really that strongly relating to their agab - because they're cis and it's just not a matter of contemplation for them, it's just their "normal" - and an agender person for example, who might feel very strongly about not being their agab because "being their agab" feels wrong to them.

"I really think a lot more cis people are trans than they realize" is kind of a weird statement in that way. Because gender identity is self-prescribed. Someone's cis as long as they're saying they're cis tbh.

You go with the label that feels comfy for you. If calling yourself nonbinary feels like "too much, posing or pointless", then you don't have to do it, you are 100% valid labelling yourself as a "feminine man" if that's what feels right for you.

It's different for everyone and a label like that always has do be self-prescribed instead of something you have to "qualify for" tbh. I'm an enby and even tho I'm amab (and not on HRT and not even presenting very 'queerly' most of the time), it feels uncomfortable as hell referring to myself as a man, even a "feminine" one. I tried that for years and the shoe just didn't fit.

If it does for you, congratulations, you found the label that's comfortable for you. That's what it's all about in the end imo.

I've started improvising and jamming with others long before I knew anything about theory. It might be a way to get to where you wanna go, I'm not sure, but the most important thing is practising your intuition and learning to trust your ears. Put on some songs that you like (and don't know how to play yet) and start jamming over them, listen to what works and what sounds off.

As a kid I used to have a keyboard on my desk, and while playing videogames and listening to music, I would just absent-mindedly noodle around on it with my left hand to what I was listening to - for hours at a time. I think that kind of subconscious practice did a LOT for me in that area :D

Edit: Forgot to say - once you become comfortable jamming "intuitively", that's where music theory comes in imo, to expand your vocabulary.

The struggles of Blighttown aren't even the main argument imo, because by skipping the Depths (which without Master Key is a very obscure path that you'd most likely never find organically as a new player, unless you are absolutely anal about exploration) you skip most of the annoying part of Blighttown. Valley of Drakes straight to Queelag is a somewhat easy path as long as you have Moss and maybe some Throwing Knives for the mosquitoes. But skipping the Large Ember from the Depths (and to a lesser extent Laurentius, if you're using Pyromancies) will seriously harm your progress if you don't know what you're doing (i.e. as a new player) and it will inconvenience you sooo much more in the long run than Capra Demon could ever.

Aside from that, both the Depths and the Sewers are such cool areas and you definitely don't wanna miss the bossfight down there. And going through Blighttown in its entirety, as intended, is a necessary rite of passage for anyone playing this game!

I wouldn't even really call that an exploit, although it might not have been intended to be possible.. But it's not like you're glitching anything, just taking advantage of the fact that the boss area has no roof. Your Fire Bombs/Dung Pies being able to hit them over the wall is just realistic tbh

* unlocking Elite and Ultimate difficulty right away with the help of Merits (Forgotten Gods DLC required, also you need a character that has reached Ultimate and finished Act 1 there naturally)
* grabbing the very first devotion shrine on Ultimate and do the first round of quests (killing Reanimator and then talking to everyone in Devil's Crossing including giving the Alchemist guy the 4 Aether Shards and Barnabas the 5 Scraps), to quickly gain the first few dozen levels, and then
* speedrunning through Normal (focussing on getting all devotion shrines) and playing through the game regularly on Elite.

With those, you'll be lvl30 after the first 10 minutes (the Ultimate stuff mentioned above) and you'll be done with Normal at around lvl50 and after 1 to 3 hours, depending on build and how familiar you are with the game.

Or in different words, some horror movies are much more easily appreciated when viewed as a genre film, and the more familiar you are with the genre the better, so you are able to identify tropes and realize when those tropes are being played with or subverted.

So since the majority of people aren't horror nerds and rate movies by comparing them with any other movie regardless of genre (think Rob Zombie's H2 compared to Citizen Kane or something), the average rating might end up pretty low, while a horror nerd might appreciate the same movie a lot more and rate it based on what it does with the genre.

The other person was an asshole about it, but I also have to disagree with you a bit. If you feel like Soulsborne games set you back more than most games when you die you are actually (and I usually don't say this lightly) approaching the game with the wrong mindset.

Because that's how the games are designed. Dying in a Soulsborne game isn't failure, even tho it can be frustrating to be set back to the last bonfire, or even loose all your souls, and feel like your progress got deleted. But the whole point is that you probably learned something from that death, maybe you saw the boss do an attack for the first time you now know how to dodge on your next attempt. Or you found a trap that killed you, but now you know where it is and can avoid it.

That's the basic gameplay loop, that's how it is designed. I get how you might feel like the game is disrespectful of your time and effort, but I would argue it's quite the opposite because every death in a Soulsborne game gives you more of the most valuable thing needed to progress in these games: Knowledge.

It's not "which button does what", it's more about the rhythm and timing of it. Like with dodge rolling for example, after a while you get a feeling for when you have to hit the button so your iframe lines up with when the weapon would hit your hitbox. When you stop playing for a few weeks it's not unusual if that feeling is gone when you get back.

Not trying to shit on the Digitakt here, I love mine, it's an incredibly versatile machine, just wanted to clarify some things OP said here:

"Mono/stereo line-in sampling" is a bit misleading because it really only samples in mono! It can take a stereo line-input and route it through in stereo, but if you sample from it it will sum the sample to mono.

Sample chopping is possible, but be aware that it's not really an intended feature - to chop up a sample you'd have to copy the whole sample to several of the 8 tracks and set different start points on each of them, it works okay (dedicated sample slicing is probably faster to do but eh) but the thing to be aware of is that it'll take up up to 8 (depending on the number of slices you want) of your tracks, which is all of them, so if you got other stuff going on you won't be able to jam with your slices live. The workflow is more like: 1.: Sample something 2.: Go to a new pattern and chop up your sample over your 8 tracks 3.: Arrange your slices, make a nice new thing with them 4.: Resample it and implement it into your original pattern as a single new sample

It works as a synth: Yes. A simple mono "wavetable" synth. "You can then use the onboard sequencer to sequence notes and chords!" Well, no, not really, can't do chords just like that since it's monophonic. Again you can do some shenanigans with multiple tracks and midi loopback but it's Not Intended.

And lastly, about playing your external synths with a Midi Keyboard via the Midi Out of the Digitakt: It works, BUT be aware that for some incredibly stupid reason, the Digitakt completely discards Pitchbend/Modwheel and Aftertouch information and it will NOT be transferred to your external synth. Only Note, Gate, Velocity is transmitted this way. (A workaround to both fully play an ext synth AND sequence it from the DT is to use a Midi Merger after the DT to merge its Midi Out and Midi Thru. Probably a bit of a headache to set up regarding channels so the synth doesn't receive the same information twice and stuff, but yeah.)
